books.section: Topic 3.12 Movement in the Early Republic

source: original; documents viewed before writing — all pre-1930 public-domain sources.
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which westward movement changed the United States in the period 1783–1800.

documents.title: Treaty of Paris
documents.source: Paraphrased from the Treaty of Paris, September 3, 1783. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A treaty between the United States and Britain, settling the borders of the new nation after the war.
documents.text: Paraphrase: In the Treaty of Paris, Britain recognized American independence and ceded the land between the Appalachian Mountains and the Mississippi River to the United States. The treaty made no provision for the Native nations who lived on that land.

documents.title: Land Ordinance of 1785
documents.source: Paraphrased from the Land Ordinance of May 20, 1785; the section 16 clause is quoted verbatim. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A law of the Confederation Congress, setting out how western land would be measured and sold.
documents.text: Paraphrase: Congress ordered the western lands surveyed into townships six miles square, each cut into thirty-six sections of 640 acres, before sale. The ordinance reserved lot number 16 of every township “for the maintenance of public schools, within the said township,” and set a minimum price of $1 an acre.

documents.title: Northwest Ordinance, Article VI
documents.source: Northwest Ordinance, July 13, 1787, Article VI. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A law of the Confederation Congress, setting the terms on which new states would join the Union.
documents.text: “There shall be neither slavery nor involuntary servitude in the said territory, otherwise than in the punishment of crimes whereof the party shall have been duly convicted: Provided, always, That any person escaping into the same, from whom labor or service is lawfully claimed in any one of the original states, such fugitive may be lawfully reclaimed and conveyed to the person claiming his or her labor or service as aforesaid.”

documents.title: Treaty of Fort Harmar
documents.source: Paraphrased from the Treaty of Fort Harmar, January 9, 1789. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A treaty made by the United States with Native leaders, showing how the government tried to gain land by agreement.
documents.text: Paraphrase: Leaders of several Native nations signed the Treaty of Fort Harmar, ceding lands north of the Ohio River to the United States. The Shawnee, who lived in the region, did not sign, and the treaty did not settle control of the Ohio country.

documents.title: United States Census, 1790
documents.source: United States Census, 1790 (United States Census Bureau). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The first federal census, counting the people of the new nation, including its western districts.
documents.text:
| 1790 census | Population |
|---|---:|
| United States, total | 3,929,214 |
| Enslaved people | 697,681 |
| Kentucky district | 73,677 |
| Southwest Territory (Tennessee) | 35,691 |

documents.title: Kentucky Admitted to the Union
documents.source: Paraphrased from the act admitting Kentucky, February 4, 1791 (1 Stat. 189); admission effective June 1, 1792. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An act of Congress admitting a new western state, the first formed from an existing state.
documents.text: Paraphrase: On June 1, 1792, Kentucky joined the Union as the fifteenth state, formed from Virginia's District of Kentucky west of the Appalachian Mountains.

documents.title: Tennessee Admitted to the Union
documents.source: Paraphrased from the 1795 territorial census of the Southwest Territory and the act admitting Tennessee, June 1, 1796. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A territorial count and an act of Congress, showing how population growth turned a territory into a state.
documents.text: Paraphrase: A territorial census in 1795 counted 77,262 people in the Southwest Territory, more than the 60,000 needed for statehood. On June 1, 1796, Tennessee joined the Union as the sixteenth state, the first formed from a federal territory.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which westward movement changed the United States in the period 1783–1800, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the new republic holding land to the Mississippi with no plan to govern it, or the weak government under the Articles of Confederation that still organized the West.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument about westward movement.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument, including documents showing both how the West changed the nation and the limits of that change.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as the cotton gin of 1793, the Wilderness Road through the Cumberland Gap, Vermont's admission in 1791, or backcountry tensions such as Shays's Rebellion.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument, such as the Treaty of Paris ignoring Native nations, the census counting settlers for representation, or the Fort Harmar treaty speaking for nations that did not sign it.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing that westward movement built equal new states while also drawing a free-slave line at the Ohio River and taking land from Native nations.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Westward movement changed the United States to a great extent between 1783 and 1800, because it added new land, new states, and new people to the Union, though it also carried slavery west and pushed Native nations off their land.
Context: Independence in 1783 left the United States with land to the Mississippi but no plan for governing it, and with a weak government under the Articles of Confederation that still managed to organize the West.
A plan for new states: Documents 2 and 3 show Congress surveying the land into townships and setting a path from territory to equal statehood, with slavery banned north of the Ohio.
Land and Native nations: Documents 1 and 4 show the United States gaining land by treaty while leaving Native nations out of the bargain, since the Treaty of Paris ignored them and the Shawnee did not sign at Fort Harmar.
People and new states: Documents 5, 6, and 7 show settlers filling Kentucky and Tennessee until their counts passed the mark for statehood, so the Union grew westward by adding states.
Outside evidence: The cotton gin of 1793 made cotton pay, so slavery spread with settlers into Kentucky and Tennessee, and the Wilderness Road of 1775 had already opened the path through the Cumberland Gap.
Complexity: The same movement that built equal new states also drew a line at the Ohio River between free and slave territory and took land from Native nations, so westward growth spread both the republic and its deepest divisions.
